identity.title: How Many Different Outputs Can a Transformer Generate?

problem.claim: Predict how many distinct output sequences a transformer can generate from a small set of architectural characteristics.

contributions.claim: Proves linear growth of maximal accessible-sequence length with prompt length, exponential decay in accessible-sequence proportion beyond a threshold, and an upper bound on the linear coefficient.
Reports an upper bound depending on prompt length that is empirically tight within a factor below 10 across architectures and model sizes.
Uses the analysis to theoretically explain reported transformer failures on copying and cramming tasks.

stated_novelty.claim: The results are presented as applying even when context and computation time are unbounded.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report empirical tightness of the prompt-length-dependent upper bound to within a factor less than 10 across architectures and model sizes.
The authors report theoretical explanations for previously observed failures on copying and cramming.
The authors report proofs of the three formal accessibility results.

narrative_sequence.summary: Studies prediction of a transformer's number of distinct output sequences using a handful of architectural characteristics.
Introduces a prompt-length-dependent upper bound and reports empirical tightness within a factor below 10 across architectures and model sizes.
Connects the analysis to previously observed failures on copying and cramming.
States linear accessible-length growth, exponential proportion decay after a threshold, and a bound on the linear coefficient.
States that these results hold even with unbounded context and computation time.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a compact architectural predictor with both a quantitative bound and formal scaling laws for accessibility.

lessons.interpretation: This pairing can make a capacity claim more interpretable by linking prediction, formal mechanism, and observable scale.
lessons.application: Structure a theory paper around one measurable quantity, then connect its predictor to a bound and explicit asymptotic laws.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the target quantity cannot be defined consistently across model architectures or sequence lengths.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify which architectural characteristics enter the predictor or the bound’s formula.
The empirical protocol, datasets, exact architectures, and meaning of “factor less than 10” are unspecified.
The critical threshold and linear coefficient are not quantified, and proof details are unavailable.
The abstract does not establish whether the proposed predictor is practically accurate beyond the reported bound comparison.
